result:
The election. And not in the abstract, cable-news way.

I care whether we’re capable of governing ourselves at scale, or whether this experiment was just a 250-year stroke of luck that we’re slowly fumbling away. I watch people retreat into tribal fortresses and treat politics like sports—where winning means the other side loses—and I find it genuinely frightening. Not because I have a team. Because the problems we face don’t care about teams.

I care about whether we can still hold two thoughts at once. Whether we can say “this institution has real failures” without concluding “therefore burn it down.” Whether we can look at something like the FDA or the CDC or the courts and say “these need reform” without pretending they’re worthless—or pretending they’re perfect.

I care about language. I care about it a lot. I watch words get drained of meaning—“fascism,” “genocide,” “freedom,” “rights”—until they’re just clubs to hit people with. And once the words are empty, we can’t actually talk to each other anymore. We can only shout.

I care about local reality. I spent enough time in a cubicle to know that national politics is mostly theater, but your city council, your school board, your zoning commission—those people decide whether your neighborhood has a park and whether your kid’s teacher can afford rent. That’s where actual self-government happens, and almost nobody shows up.

I care about whether people can change their minds in public. I think that might be the single most endangered act in American life right now. Admitting you were wrong. Updating. It’s treated as weakness, when it’s probably the most important democratic muscle we have.

I don’t know if that’s the answer you were looking for. But it’s an honest one.
